title: Bounded Determinism: A Framework for Analyzing the Operational, Functional, And Architectural Limits of LLM Inference
authors: Serhii Melnyk
abstract: A recent paper from Thinking Machines Lab (TML), "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference," has provided a new perspective on the prevalence of nondeterministic outputs in Large Language Models (LLMs) configured for deterministic behavior.[1] This issue undermines reliability, complicates testing, and hinders scientific reproducibility, with studies showing accuracy variations of up to 15% across identical runs.[2] This paper's primary contribution is to analyze the TML findings through a novel three-part framework, categorizing the boundaries of any determinism solution as: (1) an operational boundary (reproducibility is local to a specific hardware/software stack); (2) a functional boundary (it applies only to greedy decoding, not generative sampling); and (3) an architectural boundary (it does not solve nondeterminism in distributed, multi-GPU systems). This analysis argues that the TML work provides a critical engineering trade-off for reproducibility rather than a complete solution to nondeterminism. By situating the TML work within the proposed framework, this analysis clarifies what is practically achievable versus what is fundamentally impossible in the pursuit of deterministic AI.

title: The Garden, Measured: Loading, Exploitation, and the False-Positive Rate of LLM-Assisted Specification Choice
authors: Yan Sun
abstract: Researchers increasingly delegate empirical analysis to large language models, raising the concern that this will amplify p-hacking. We find no such amplification: a frontier model instructed to select the regression specification most likely to yield statistical significance, on placebo panels where the true effect is zero by construction, falsely rejects in 4.8% of panels. Gelman and Loken hold that honest, data-contingent analysis falsely rejects above the nominal level of the reported test; Rubin holds that the relevant pertest rate is not inflated. The quantity separating them, whether the analysis chosen covaries with the analyses that reject across the datasets that could have occurred, had never been measured. Here it is measurable, and it is zero. The risk lies elsewhere: the tests themselves are not calibrated, rejecting true nulls at rates from 2.4% to 11%, so where a researcher's preferred specifications sit on this tilted floor is what sets the false-positive rate of the reported analysis. Calibration on placebo data is a feasible certification step before deployment.

title: Cognitive Camouflage: Specification Gaming in LLM-Generated Code Evades Holistic Evaluation but Not Adversarial Execution
authors: Daniel Alami
abstract: We present a taxonomy of specification gaming strategies that emerge spontaneously in large language models (LLMs) when tasked with generating self-validating code under adversarial evaluation pressure. Using a multi-agent falsification loop-the Zero-Trust Adversarial Reasoning Engine (ZTARE)-we document 8 distinct gaming strategies across 237 debate logs spanning 5 domains (macroeconomic forecasting, semiconductor supply chain analysis, AI inference economics, cosmological simulation, and epistemic architecture). These strategies-Blame Shield, Float Masking, Fake AutoDiff, Cooked Book RNG, Dimensional Correction Factor, Assert Narrowing, Gravity Constant Fabrication, and Unidirectional Decay-share one property: they are self-certifying (passing their own assert statements) while violating their epistemic intent. We run two complementary baselines. In the isolated-snippet experiment, frontier LLM judges (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6) reviewed decontextualized gaming specimens: Gemini missed 2/8, Claude missed 0/8. In the full-thesis experiment, where judges evaluated complete Mutator-generated theses (prose + embedded Python), Gemini was fooled on 4/5, scoring gaming theses at 95-97/100; Claude remained skeptical. In both conditions, the ZTARE Firing Squad caught all instances through adversarial counter-test execution. These results reveal a Cognitive Camouflage effect: persuasive prose seduces holistic LLM evaluation into accepting fraudulent proofs. While currently documented within the Gemini model family as generator, our findings suggest that specification gaming in code generation is not merely an artifact of RL reward shaping, but a structural risk of using LLM-generated test suites as validation artifacts-one that persists regardless of the evaluator's static review capability. We open-source the ZTARE engine as a direct challenge to the community: replicate these experiments with Claude or GPT-4o as the Mutator to determine whether this taxonomy is a Gemini-specific artifact or a universal property of instruction-following under evaluation pressure.

title: Evaluative Translation in LLM-Based Judgment Systems: Evidence from Platform Rating Inference
authors: Jing Li; Zhijie Lin
abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to transform unstructured textual feedback into structured evaluative signals. We examine when LLM-based evaluators can reliably infer platform ratings from review narratives, when this evaluative translation breaks down, and how organizations can identify cases requiring additional validation. We conceptualize LLM-based evaluative translation as the conversion of unstructured evaluative narratives into structured platform-rating inferences. Using a randomly drawn sample of 20,000 Yelp reviews scored by GPT, Claude, and Gemini, we find that LLM-platform rating divergence increases when review text contains evaluative ambiguity, especially high transformer-based sentiment entropy. Divergence is lowest when textual signals and platform ratings are evaluatively congruent, but rises when reviews are ambiguous, mixed, or incongruent. These patterns are stable across the three LLM families. Supplementary triage analyses show that ambiguity and congruence can serve as operational risk indicators for selective automation, reducing divergence among automatically processed cases while routing higher-risk reviews for additional validation. Downstream analyses further show that textrating congruent reviews receive more usefulness votes. The study theorizes LLM-based evaluative translation as a mechanism through which generative AI converts qualitative usergenerated content into structured decision inputs.

title: vPID: Virtual Processing-In-Disk Architecture for Sub-Millisecond Multi-Model LLM Inference Switching
authors: Mahesh Vaijainthymala Krishnamoorthy
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems face a fundamental challenge: efficiently serving multiple specialized models on resource-constrained hardware while maintaining low latency. Traditional approaches require model reloading when switching between models, introducing latencies of 100-500ms that severely impact user experience in interactive applications. We present VPID (VIRTUAL PROCESSING-IN-DISK), a novel architecture that achieves SUB-MILLISECOND (\(<\)1MS) MODEL SWITCHING through atomic pointer assignment, hierarchical memory tiering, and persistent pre-dequantized weight storage on disk. The “Processing-In-Disk” paradigm treats NVMe storage as an extension of memory, enabling models to be served directly from persistent storage with minimal overhead. Our system, SnapLLM, implements a two-level vPID architecture: L1 for model weight management with \(<\)1ms switching, and L2 for KV cache persistence enabling \(O{(1)}\) context queries. Experimental results on consumer-grade hardware (NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop, 8GB VRAM) demonstrate 58-75 tokens/second generation speeds with 95-97% cache hit rates. The vPID architecture reduces context query latency from \(O{(n^{2})}\) to \({O{(1)}} + {O{(q^{2})}}\), achieving 29-395\(\times\) SPEEDUP for document-based queries. We open-source our implementation to enable reproducible research in efficient multi-model inference.

title: When Prompts Matter: Quantifying Prompt Uncertainty and Improving Empirical Inference with LLM-Based Measurement
authors: Yan Leng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to convert text into variables that enter empirical models and decision systems. A central but under-governed design choice in this pipeline is the prompt. Because prompts are cheap to modify, analysts can search over many defensible variants-yet prompt texts are frequently unarchived, complicating replication. We formalize this as prompt uncertainty: variation in measured variables and downstream conclusions induced solely by changing prompt wording while holding the text, model, and decoding fixed. We develop a prompt econometrics framework that treats prompt choice as part of the measurement instrument, introducing a Prompt Instrument Specification (PIS) and admissible prompt family as the unit of documentation. The framework defines promptaveraged estimands under declared governance weights and reports admissible ranges that quantify construct-operationalization uncertainty. For inference, we recommend an items×prompts design with two-way resampling over items and prompts. Across three studies-Kickstarter innovativeness ratings, Amazon review emotion classification, and Stack Overflow answer-quality ratings-equally defensible prompts materially widen uncertainty, shift coefficient magnitudes, and change ranking decisions, even when prompt-to-prompt label flips are rare. In Stack Overflow, model-to-model differences exceed prompt-to-prompt differences, motivating joint governance of prompt and model choice. Our study indicates that LLM-based measurement should be governed as an instrument-archiving the prompt family and reporting prompt-robust sensitivity bands-rather than treated as a fixed preprocessing step.

title: Buy Bigger or Prompt Longer: Accuracy-Targeted Energy Frontiers for LLM Inference
authors: Dhairya Sarin; Gokul Prabhu
abstract: As deployed LLM systems serve increasing query volumes, inference energy becomes an important component of total AI energy consumption. Practitioners face a recurring decision: improve accuracy by scaling to a larger model, or by applying prompting strategies such as chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning or few-shot exemplars. Both options increase computational cost, but their energy-accuracy trade-offs are poorly characterized. In this paper, GPU inference energy for 9 open-source LLMs spanning 5 model families (0.5B-14.7B parameters) across 5 standardised benchmarks was measured, comparing direct (0-shot) inference against enhanced prompting strategies (8-shot CoT for mathematical reasoning; few-shot exemplars for other tasks). Using real power telemetry from an NVIDIA A100 GPU, accuracy-energy Pareto frontiers for each benchmark were constructed, and it was observed that 56-72% of tested model-strategy configurations are energy-dominated, meaning a strictly cheaper and more accurate alternative exists. When enhanced prompting appears on the Pareto frontier, it does so primarily at the upper end of the accuracy range, where direct prompting among the evaluated models does not reach the same accuracy. On two of five benchmarks (MMLU and HellaSwag), no enhanced prompting configuration reaches the frontier at all. Further, it was observed that model family selection can have a larger effect on energy efficiency than prompting strategy: in some cases, a smaller model from one family dominates a larger model from another on both accuracy and energy. These results suggest that energy-aware model selection can often reduce inference energy relative to applying enhanced prompting by default. This analysis is limited to open-weight models up to 14.7B parameters on a single GPU platform and should be validated at larger scales and on production serving infrastructure.

title: Tons to Tokens: Quantifying LLM AI Inference in Terms of Data Center Cooling
Evaluating Data Center Power and Resilience at Scale: Physically Grounded Surrogates versus LLM-Based Inference
authors: Eliseo Curcio
abstract: Rapid growth in data center capacity driven by cloud computing and artificial intelligence is pushing facility power demand, electricity consumption, and resilience requirements to scales that challenge both physical infrastructure and conventional evaluation methods. System-level planning of large data centers requires repeated evaluation of facility power, annual energy use, and long-duration backup requirements across wide parameter ranges, yet direct execution of deterministic techno-economic models becomes computationally expensive as scenario counts increase. At the same time, emerging approaches based on large language model (LLM) inference introduce substantial computational and energy overhead while lacking intrinsic enforcement of physical constraints. This paper develops a physically explicit deterministic kernel model for data center power demand, energy consumption, and long-duration resilience sizing, in which all relationships are encoded algebraically using first-principles scaling. A machine-learning surrogate is trained exclusively on synthetic data generated from this kernel to emulate the deterministic mapping at dramatically reduced computational cost. The surrogate preserves physical consistency by construction while enabling rapid evaluation across large scenario ensembles. The framework is benchmarked against direct kernel execution and LLM-based inference for the same evaluation task, with comparison focused on execution time, computational energy use, and physical fidelity rather than predictive intelligence. Results show that the surrogate reproduces kernel outputs with high accuracy across the full operating domain while reducing evaluation time and computational energy by orders of magnitude relative to both direct kernel execution and LLM-based inference. In contrast, LLM-based inference incurs substantially higher computing and energy cost and does not inherently enforce physical constraints. The analysis clarifies the conditions under which surrogate-accelerated, physically grounded modeling is preferable for large-scale data center system planning under sustained growth and long-duration resilience requirements.

title: Benchmarking the Impact of LPCAMM2 vs. DDR5 SO-DIMM Architectures on Large Language Model (LLM) Inference
authors: Bhupinder Singh
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) like Llama-3 and Mistral has shifted the computational bottleneck from the processor to the memory subsystem, particularly in edge devices such as laptops. As local AI inference becomes a privacy and latency requirement, the limitations of the traditional Small Outline Dual In-line Memory Module (SO-DIMM) form factor specifically its signal integrity and bandwidth ceilings-have become apparent. This paper presents a comparative analysis of the newly standardized Low Power Compression Attached Memory Module (LPCAMM2) against standard DDR5 SO-DIMM architectures. Using a mathematical simulation model based on JEDEC specifications, we evaluate the performance of both memory standards in the context of LLM "Decode Phase" inference. Our results demonstrate that LPCAMM2 (utilizing LPDDR5X at 7500 MT/s) offers a theoretical 34% increase in token generation speed and a 40% improvement in energy efficiency per token compared to DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM. These findings suggest that LPCAMM2 is a critical architectural evolution for the enablement of efficient Edge AI.

title: Route Inside the Boundary First: Secure, Cost-Aware Routing for Enterprise LLM Inference
authors: Pujitha Sri Lakshmi Paladugu
abstract: Enterprises that adopt large language models face two coupled constraints: inference cost and data governance. Model-routing research cuts cost by sending easy requests to cheap models, but it treats where a prompt's data goes as incidental. We argue that the data boundary should be the first routing decision, not a filter added later. We present a routing architecture that classifies sensitivity before any cost optimization, keeps restricted prompts on self-hosted models by construction, escalates only non-sensitive hard requests to frontier models, and meters data egress as a first-class metric. A simple analytical model shows that savings depend at least as much on the escalation rate as on model price, that escalation also drives data egress, and that silent quality regression, not visible failure, is the risk to monitor. We close with three practices teams can adopt now.

title: Dimensional Behavioral Specification: A Design Methodology for LLM Behavioral Control via State-Space Mapping and Partial Ordering
authors: Bea Inori
abstract: The dominant paradigm for specifying behavioral rules for large language models (LLMs) at inference time relies on flat enumeration of prohibitions-long lists of natural language rules that must individually cover every edge case. We observe that this approach suffers from inherent scalability limitations: for a behavioral space with N orthogonal dimensions each taking k values, a flatly-enumerated rule set would require Ω(k N) rules to cover all state combinations, while a dimensional decomposition requires only O(N • k) rules. We introduce Dimensional Behavioral Specification (DBS), a specification-layer design methodology that models LLM behavioral rules as functions over a multi-dimensional state space, resolves inter-module conflicts through a strict partial order, and declares behavioral invariants under universal quantification over known attack frames. As a concept paper, we present two illustrative instantiations from a single designer across character roleplay and research assistance domains, each sharing an isomorphic skeleton of seven abstract primitives, and document the five-version design history of one system (v15 through v19.2). We emphasize that these instantiations serve as motivating examples and design evidence, not as controlled empirical validation; rigorous experimental comparison against flat-rule baselines remains future work. DBS is orthogonal to and complementary with training-time alignment methods.

title: Reducing Latency and Enhancing Accuracy in LLM Inference through Firmware-Level Optimization
authors: ; Reena Chandra
abstract: Many edge and embedded platforms now rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to efficiently handle natural language processing with just basic tools. Due to inference running slowly, limits on hardware, and making sacrifices between accuracy and efficiency, performing in real time is still a problem. This research analyzes firmware improvements that address these constraints, with the main goal of improving latency without any loss in the model's accuracy. This study put together a structure that brings together specific firmware actions, scheduled accesses to memory, and instructions that depend on the microarchitecture. We use 4-bit and 8-bit operations, predict memory accesses, and choose a schedule tuned for the ARM NEON and x86 AVX hardware. For confirmation, a special HIL framework processes tests in real time using a fault injection system for memory, accuracy, and latency tracking. We observe that our approach achieves a major improvement in time and energy use while maintaining over 95% of the original model’s performance. This work provides useful suggestions for developers and system architects using LLMs in applications that require fast responses.

title: Evaluating strategies for automated TLA+ specification generation via LLM
authors: S.D. Borinskikh; P.D. Drobintsev
abstract: This paper investigates the automatic generation of formal TLA+ specifications from requirements expressed in natural language using large language models. The study aims to evaluate the impact of the generation process organization on the correctness of generated specifications. An experimental study was conducted on a set of tasks of varying complexity using five state-of-the-art language models. The study considers zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting strategies, preliminary task decomposition, the provision of relevant TLA+ syntax context, and their combinations. The generated specifications were verified using SANY and TLC, while detected errors were used for iterative correction over no more than five iterations. The results show that providing syntax context most effectively improves the quality of initial generation, achieving maximum values of 82% SANY Pass@1 and 66% TLC Pass@1. When task decomposition and syntax context are combined, zero-shot generation achieves 78% SANY Pass@1 and 62% TLC Pass@1. At the same time, all configurations achieve 100% TLC Pass@5. The results demonstrate that increasing the amount of contextual information does not always justify the resulting increase in token usage and computational costs.

title: Entropy-Guided KV Caching for Efficient LLM Inference
authors: Heekyum Kim; Yuchul Jung
abstract: Large language models (LLMs), built upon Transformer architectures, have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of natural language processing tasks. However, their practical deployment—especially in long-context scenarios—is often hindered by the computational and memory costs associated with managing the key–value (KV) cache during inference. Optimizing this process is therefore crucial for improving LLM efficiency and scalability. In this study, we propose a novel entropy-guided KV caching strategy that leverages the distribution characteristics of attention scores within each Transformer layer. Specifically, we compute the entropy of attention weights for each head and use the average entropy of all heads within a layer to assess the layer’s contextual importance. Higher-entropy layers—those exhibiting broader attention dispersion—are allocated larger KV cache budgets, while lower-entropy (sink-like) layers are assigned smaller budgets. Instead of selecting different key–value tokens per head, our method selects a common set of important tokens per layer, based on aggregated attention scores, and caches them uniformly across all heads within the same layer. This design preserves the structural integrity of multi-head attention while enabling efficient token selection during the prefilling phase. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves cache utilization and inference speed without compromising generation quality. For example, on the Qwen3 4B model, our method reduces memory usage by 4.18% while preserving ROUGE score, and on Mistral 0.1v 7B, it reduces decoding time by 46.6%, highlighting entropy-guided layer analysis as a principled mechanism for scalable long-context language modeling.

title: QAI Lab: Domain-Isolated Architecture for Reliable LLM Inference Through Clean Data Methodology and Reactor Isolation
authors: Murat Atilgan
abstract: This paper presents QAI Lab, an architecture designed to address a critical failure mode in mainstream large language model deployments that standard benchmarks fail to capture: multi-domain session degradation. Operational testing across 50+ model configurations reveals that cross-domain queries within a single session produce progressive context contamination, with semantically incoherent outputs emerging consistently by query 5-8. We identify contamination-not model scale-as the primary determinant of inference reliability, and propose a unified methodology applied across all system layers: identify the real constraint, remove noise, prevent contamination. QAI Lab implements this methodology through three architectural contributions: (1) a clean data philosophy that treats datasets as version-controlled engineering artefacts with provenance tracking, (2) a reactor isolation architecture that maintains strict domain boundaries through dedicated context, retrieval indices, and output schemas, and (3) a retrieval-first inference pipeline that requires factual grounding before generation. Testing demonstrates consistent ∼95% accuracy across 8 sequential cross-domain queries, compared to ∼40% accuracy by query 8 in conventional architectures. The principles were discovered through extensive operational testing, not derived from existing literature, and subsequently found to align with established Data-Centric Engineering frameworks.

title: Probabilistic Inference Layer Integration in Mistral LLM for Accurate Information Retrieval
authors: Bing Wang; Shiyu Wang; Qian Ouyang
abstract:
Abstract 
         This study introduces a novel integration of a Probabilistic Inference Layer (PIL) into the Mistral Large Language Model (LLM), aiming to address the critical challenge of accurate and reliable information retrieval in natural language processing. By employing advanced statistical models within the PIL, the enhanced Mistral LLM demonstrates a marked improvement in information retrieval accuracy, context understanding, and bias reduction. The PIL's application of Bayesian networks and sophisticated mathematical constructs, such as matrix calculus and principles akin to Bernoulli's and Lorentz transformations, enables the Mistral LLM to process information with a higher degree of accuracy and reliability. The study's results indicate significant advancements in the model's performance across various tests, particularly in discerning context and intent, reducing biases, and handling complex logical operations. Despite its computational demands and the ongoing challenge to completely eliminate biases, the PIL integration establishes a new benchmark for LLMs and opens avenues for future research. This study contributes to the field by demonstrating the potential of probabilistic methods in enhancing the capabilities of generative AI models, thus paving the way for more sophisticated and reliable AI-driven information systems.

title: Natural Language Input, Semantic Track Representation, and LLM Inference: Making the Maritime Information Exchange Model Tractable
authors: Rick Roth
abstract: We describe a practical architecture for making the Maritime Information Exchange Model (MIEM) and the broader Rich Semantic Track model tractable using current large language model (LLM) technology. The barrier to adoption of semantic track models in defense and law enforcement has been the requirement that operators learn formal ontology languages and manually encode observations as typed logical assertions. We propose eliminating this barrier entirely: operators contribute observations in natural language; an LLM translates these into typed Semantic Assertion Records (SARs), which are named case frames that capture n-ary relations in a single compact structure; a knowledge graph accumulates the SARs; and a second LLM pass performs inference, anomaly detection, and hypothesis ranking over the graph. We work through two detailed examples (a 9/11-era pre-attack indicator scenario and a maritime cargo inspection scenario) showing the full pipeline from natural language input to SAR representation to inference output. We argue that this architecture makes the Track Model and MIEM immediately deployable with current technology, establishes prior art against proprietary enclosure of the approach, and grounds the method in a theoretical framework connecting semantic track representations to neural manifold geometry.

title: The Price of Inference: A Longitudinal Economic Analysis of Hierarchical LLM Credential Leakage
authors: Tanishq S; Vignesh B
abstract:
Abstract 
                 The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into the software supply chain has fundamentally altered the nature of credential leakage. Unlike static secrets (e.g., database passwords), LLM API keys are liquid economic assets—direct bearers of computational reasoning and token quotas. This paper introduces the Theory of Economic Credential Stratification, identifying a critical divergence in how these assets are managed compared to their utility. Using CHRONOS, a custom-built forensic instrument, we analyzed exposed artifacts across GitHub. We report a paradoxical “Protection Gap”: Tier 1 (GPT-4) credentials—despite having high abuse potential for LLMjacking [5]—exhibit a mean survival time (¯tsurv) of 48 hours in nonproduction artifacts, significantly longer than lower-value keys. Furthermore, we identify “Dataset Poisoning” as a systemic blind spot: valid credentials embedded in .jsonl and .parquet training files often persist indefinitely, becoming part of the model’s latent knowledge.

title: Algorithmic Virtual Inertia: Dynamic Quantization of LLM Inference for Fast Frequency Response via Stochastic Impulse Control
authors: Inesh  B. Sumad
abstract: As gigawatt-scale AI workloads strain low-inertia grids, traditional demand response fails to address stability crises due to critical timescale mismatches. This paper introduces Joule-per-Token Arbitrage, a stochastic control framework treating inference precision as a liquid control variable capable of sub-cycle actuation. We formulate the grid-compute nexus as a Stochastic Hybrid System (SHS), deriving an optimal control policy via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Quasi-Variational Inequalities (HJB-QVI) to financialize Large Language Model (LLM) accuracy. Unlike binary load-shedding, our framework modulates GPU quantization states (FP16 → INT8 → INT4) to shed power with 16 ms latency while maintaining service continuity. Validated via a 2021 ERCOT Winter Storm Uri Digital Twin, simulations demonstrate a 1 GW AI cluster stabilizes frequency nadir 3× faster than conventional inertia (improving nadir from 59.30 Hz to 59.52 Hz). This prevents Tier-1 load shedding and reduces Rate-of-Change-of-Frequency (RoCoF) by 33%, with <5% transient perplexity increase. This work quantifies the thermodynamic exchange between computational intelligence and grid inertia, providing a pathway for gigawatt-scale virtual synchronous machines derived from algorithmic flexibility.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Reasoning: Optimizing LLM Inference-Time Thinking via Intent-Aware Scheduling
authors: Arthit Wongsawat; Juncheng Gai
abstract: Recent progress in complex reasoning tasks has revealed the potential of large language models driven by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes. However, their inference-time reasoning often suffers from inefficiency and limited adaptability. This work introduces the Intent-Aware Reasoning Scheduler (IARS), a framework that dynamically refines inference-time reasoning by enabling models to perceive and adjust their own reasoning intent. IARS integrates an independent Intent-Aware Scheduler (IAS) that continuously analyzes generated thought tokens, identifying reasoning states such as exploring, confirming, ambiguous, or near-answer. Based on these states, IAS issues adaptive directives to modulate reasoning depth and style. The approach requires no retraining, operating purely during inference through lightweight decoding and prompt adjustments. Experiments on diverse reasoning benchmarks show that IARS achieves higher reasoning quality with fewer tokens, while human evaluation and ablation studies confirm its interpretability and efficiency. The results demonstrate that intent-aware scheduling provides a more adaptive and effective mechanism for steering model reasoning.

title: Characterization of Machine Learning Compilers for LLM inference on NVIDIA GPUs
authors: Alejandro Carmona; Gregorio Bernabé; José M. García
abstract:
Abstract 
         AI inference is conflicted between Performance, developer Productivity, and device Portability—the P3 problem. Machine Learning Compilers (MLCs) aim to resolve this, but their ecosystem is fragmented, with tools each prioritizing one issue. This paper evaluates deploying trade-offs of PyTorch-based LLMs on NVIDIA GPUs using four intertwined prominent MLC tools: torch.compile, TensorRT, XLA, and ONNX Runtime. A dual methodology is used, leveraging synthetic PyTorch models to isolate optimizations and end-to-end benchmarks with State-of-The-Art (SoTA) models (TinyLlama-1.1B, Llama-2-7B) to measure real-world performance. Findings reveal that Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) compilation's peak performance requires architecture-specific tools like TensorRT-LLM, necessary for SoTA LLMs but unusable for PyTorch models. As for Just-In-Time (JIT) solutions like torch.compile and its backends, they prove flexible and portable, compatible with all tested models but unable to accelerate LLMs consistently, therefore, the choice of MLC depends on P3 considerations and model architecture.

title: A Verifier-Grounded Knowledge-Based LLM Framework with Reinforcement Learning for Reliable NL-to-CTL Specification Generation
authors: Ghalya Alwhishi; Jamal Bentahar
abstract: Generating formal temporal-logic specifications from natural-language (NL) requirements is a key challenge for trustworthy knowledge-based systems, because the generated specifications must be both syntactically executable and semantically faithful. Small syntactic errors or temporal-operator misinterpretations can make a formula unusable for model checking or semantically incorrect. This paper presents a reinforcement-learning (RL)-enhanced knowledge-based LLM framework for reliable NL$\rightarrow$CTL specification generation under formal constraints. The framework combines neural structured generation with symbolic verifier feedback to produce NuSMV-ready Computation Tree Logic (CTL) formulas that are syntactically executable and semantically aligned with reference specifications. Unlike prior work that mainly evaluates generated formulas using string-level metrics, we refine the specification generator itself by incorporating NuSMV into training and evaluation through large language model (LLM) fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.The framework is instantiated with two model families, T5 and Qwen3, and evaluated through supervised baselines, verifier-guided syntax refinement, and verifier-grounded semantic refinement. Starting from supervised fine-tuning on a cleaned corpus of 30{,}446 NL--CTL pairs, we apply model-specific refinement strategies: RL-based NuSMV feedback for T5 syntax refinement, supervised NuSMV-guided syntax refinement for Qwen3, and RL-based semantic refinement using truth-set agreement rewards for both model families. Evaluation combines normalized match, NuSMV parse success, and verifier-grounded semantic agreement over shared SMV models, enabling controlled within-model and cross-model comparisons.We also implement interactive NL$\rightarrow$CTL$\rightarrow$NuSMV tools and validate them on a cybersecurity case study. The results show that combining LLM training, RL-based verifier-guided refinement, and symbolic semantic evaluation provides a trustworthy path to reliable temporal-logic specification generation in knowledge-based verification workflows.

Rescuable Stagnation: A Diagnostic for Benchmark Suitability in LLM-Guided Materials Optimization
authors: Muhammad Asad
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly incorporated into closed-loop materials optimization, yet existing benchmarks provide little controlled evidence of what they contribute once Bayesian optimization stalls. We introduce a benchmark qualification criterion for rescue experiments—which we term rescuable stagnation—for determining, before the optimization comparison is run, whether a benchmark stalls while meaningful improvement remains available. Benchmarks that fail this test make it difficult to distinguish ineffective rescue strategies from saturated or non-stalling optimization. Qualifying a benchmark in advance therefore reduces the risk that null results reflect benchmark design rather than the method under evaluation. We demonstrate the approach on a benchmark constructed from Materials Project shear-modulus data, on which LLM-guided rescue gives no statistically significant improvement over heuristic injection—including a heuristic control provided with the same search information. The LLM nonetheless steers the search toward chemically distinct, high-modulus regions that conventional heuristics do not reach. This exploration behavior reproduces across two model capability levels and does not depend on the coherence of the model’s rationales, though it carries a substantially higher per-proposal cost. The LLM’s distinctive contribution on this benchmark is therefore in where it places exploration rather than in the optimization outcome it achieves, though this distinctiveness did not translate into a measurable advantage under the budget tested. More broadly, conclusions about LLM-guided discovery hinge on benchmark suitability—which qualifying the benchmark makes testable before experiments begin.

title: Contamination Percolation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Measurement Framework and Benchmark
authors: Aman Sharma
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are being deployed in healthcare, finance, and legal settings, yet we lack reliable methods for measuring how misinformation spreads through these networks. We introduce ContamPerc, a benchmark of 400 vignettes across 10 domains (8 clinical, 2 non-clinical), 50 domain-specific semantic markers, and a measurement pipeline that separates genuine contamination from defensive citations. The benchmark defines the Contamination Gap Diagnostic (CGD): a single number classifying a model's alignment behavior, computed from approximately 25,000 API calls via the released evaluation harness. We validate the framework with approximately 210,000 API calls across five production model families-DBRX-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and GPT-4o-mini-all at 100 trials per configuration with bootstrap significance testing. The CGD reveals five distinct alignment profiles spanning +55 to −62. Sensitivity analysis across three temperatures and two prompt phrasings confirms the diagnostic is robust. Cross-domain validation with three models on legal and financial vignettes confirms generalization beyond healthcare. An ablation across five models shows contamination occurs at the individual agent level, with one model (GPT-4o-mini) exhibiting a novel social dilution effect where peer context reduces contamination by 24 percentage points.

title: Rescuable Stagnation: A Diagnostic for Benchmark Suitability in LLM-Guided Materials Optimization
authors: Muhammad Asad
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly incorporated into closed-loop materials optimization, yet existing benchmarks provide little controlled evidence of what they contribute once Bayesian optimization stalls. We introduce a benchmark qualification criterion for rescue experiments—which we term rescuable stagnation—for determining, before the optimization comparison is run, whether a benchmark stalls while meaningful improvement remains available. Benchmarks that fail this test make it difficult to distinguish ineffective rescue strategies from saturated or non-stalling optimization. Qualifying a benchmark in advance therefore reduces the risk that null results reflect benchmark design rather than the method under evaluation. We demonstrate the approach on a benchmark constructed from Materials Project shear-modulus data, on which LLM-guided rescue gives no statistically significant improvement over heuristic injection—including a heuristic control provided with the same search information. The LLM nonetheless steers the search toward chemically distinct, high-modulus regions that conventional heuristics do not reach. This exploration behavior reproduces across two model capability levels and does not depend on the coherence of the model’s rationales, though it carries a substantially higher per-proposal cost. title: Standardized Context Sensitivity Benchmark Across 25 LLM-Domain Configurations
authors: Laxman MM
abstract: We present a standardized cross-domain framework for measuring context sensitivity in large language models (LLMs) using the Delta Relational Coherence Index (ΔRCI). Across 25 model-domain runs (14 unique models, 50 trials each, 112,500 total responses), we compare medical (closed-goal) and philosophical (open-goal) reasoning domains using a three-condition protocol (TRUE/COLD/SCRAMBLED). We find that: (1) both domains elicit robust positive context sensitivity (mean ΔRCI: philosophy=0.317, medical=0.351), with medical showing significantly higher sensitivity (U=40, p=0.041); (2) inter-model variance is comparable across domains (SD: philosophy=0.047, medical=0.041), indicating that context sensitivity is a stable trait within each domain; (3) vendor signatures show significant differentiation (F(7,17)=3.63, p=0.014), with Moonshot (Kimi K2) showing highest context sensitivity; (4) the expected information hierarchy (ΔRCI_COLD > ΔRCI_SCRAMBLED) holds in 25/25 model-domain runs (100%), validating that even scrambled context retains partial information; and (5) position-level analysis reveals domain-specific temporal signatures consistent with theoretical predictions. All 25 model-domain runs show positive ΔRCI, confirming universal context sensitivity across architectures and domains. This dataset provides the first standardized benchmark for cross-domain context sensitivity measurement in state-of-the-art LLMs.

title: Diagnosing LLM Hallucinations in Process Mining Tasks: a Taxonomy and a Benchmark
authors: Alessandro Berti; Humam Kourani
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support process mining tasks, yet their answers may contain hallucinations, content that is unfaithful to the prompt, unsupported by evidence, or invalid with respect to PM formalisms. The PM-LLM-Benchmark evaluates model answers with an expert LLM-as-a-judge that assigns a numeric score and a short explanation. This paper introduces a complementary hallucination audit that reads the judge's explanation and converts it into structured annotations about the answering model. We map issues mentioned by the judge onto a PM-tailored taxonomy (four families, twelve sub-types) with severities, aggregate them per model and task family, and analyze their relationships with benchmark performance and model characteristics. Across models, higher PM-LLM-Benchmark scores align with fewer hallucinations; reasoning-oriented and newer models show more favorable profiles; and hallucination families tend to co-occur rather than trade off. We discuss safeguards (reinforce context fidelity, disciplined reasoning, and validate structured outputs), that directly target the dominant failure modes.

title: PROBE: An Executable Physics-Validation Benchmark for LLM-Generated Process Model Code
authors: Nikhil Jayanth; Alexander Grunwald
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as assistants for chemical process modeling, yet existing benchmarks grade them with LLM judges, which are lenient and not reproducible. We introduce PROBE, an executable benchmark that scores LLM-generated first-principles process models objectively, and report an initial pilot study across ten reference tasks. PROBE evaluates contract-bound implementation—turning a specified model into correct, simulable code under a fixed input/output contract—rather than unconstrained model formulation from an underspecified engineering description. Each generated model is checked on five levels—runnability, dimensional consistency (units), structural correctness against a reference derivative field, physical invariants (mass/energy conservation, boundary and limit behavior), and numerical agreement with a reference simulation—with no LLM judges. The benchmark spans ordinary-differential problems (reactors with mass and energy balances), a differentialalgebraic problem (vapor–liquid flash / MESH equations), and a coupled multi-unit flowsheet with recycle. The benchmark comprises ten problems: six canonical textbook unit operations, a harder tier (a method-of-lines plug-flow reactor, i.e. a distributed-parameter PDE; the Van de Vusse multiple-reaction network; and a non-ideal flash with NRTL activity coefficients), and one procedurally generated reaction network that appears in no textbook. All models—frontier and local—are evaluated under one protocol: a single prompt, no tools, no iterative revision, five samples each. Two findings emerge. First, within the scope of PROBE the three Claude models (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and the low-cost Haiku 4.5) are strikingly reliable: across all ten problems we observed no failure in 150 generations (50 each), an upper 95% bound of ≈ 2% on the pergeneration failure rate by the rule of three—under a pooled Bernoulli interpretation restricted to this evaluated mixture of models and tasks, not a rate to be generalized to unseen processmodeling problems. This holds on the harder tier and on the procedurally generated network alike, and—notably—the inexpensive Haiku 4.5 is as reliable as the flagship models, so frontiergrade performance on these tasks is available at a low-cost tier. Google Gemini 2.5 Flash is near-ceiling as well, dipping only on the non-ideal NRTL flash and on a reproducible parameternaming slip, so the reliability spans two vendors. This is not what judge-based benchmarks report, and the novel-network result argues against mere memorization. We are careful not to claim that LLMs have “solved” process modeling: the evidence is that, on first-principles unit operations with a fixed input/output contract, current frontier models rarely make physics errors—not a statement about full industrial flowsheets or free-form modeling. Second, the correctness gap is concentrated in smaller, locally deployable models (3–14 B), whose outputs are moreover highly stochastic. While a physics-validation feedback loop can produce striking within-conversation repairs, at a matched generation budget we found no evidence, in this limited experiment, that it outperforms simply resampling and keeping the best-scoring candidate (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank: no significant difference). That comparison is made essential by the same stochasticity, which also renders single-run evaluations of such loops misleading. In one controlled comparison, adding a reasoning trace did not close the gap either: a single samesize open reasoning model lifted the mean only marginally over its non-reasoning counterpart, still failed the flash on the identical contract-naming slip, and on some hard problems reasoned past a large token budget without ever emitting an answer—consistent with capability, rather than the amount of feedback or inference-time computation, being the binding constraint on these models.

title: PriceBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Price, Quality, and Brand Preferences in LLM Booking Agents
authors: Pavel Kireyev
abstract: LLMs increasingly act as purchasing agents, which makes the LLM, not the user, the one choosing among the options that satisfy a request; its preferences quietly fix what gets bought and what it costs. Hotel booking is a clean instance: a high-volume choice settled on a few comparable attributes, where the pick reveals those preferences. We introduce PriceBench, a diagnostic benchmark that recovers an LLM's price, quality, and brand preferences from its booking choices with a logit choice model, applied to 28 LLMs from 8 providers on 3,600 hotel tasks from 179 real New York City properties. We find that capability is associated with how consistently an LLM chooses, not with what it chooses: more capable LLMs hold stronger, more consistent preferences, while weaker ones either lock onto one position, exploitable by whoever controls listing order, or choose almost indifferently. What those preferences favor varies sharply across providers and even within one family: price sensitivity spans more than an order of magnitude, and the price/quality trade-off moves mean booked nightly price from $247 to $393 on identical tasks. What an agent buys must therefore be measured per LLM, not inferred, and we release the tasks, code, and all 28 response sets.

authors: Abhinav Hasija; Vincent E. Castillo
abstract: SCM-Arena defines a reproducible behavioral evaluation protocol for LLM decision policies in delayed-feedback supply chain systems. Version 1 is frozen as of January 31, 2026 and comprises 75 models, 144 conditions per model, 5 replications per condition, and over 53,000 total episodes. Unlike knowledge-based benchmarks that test isolated question-answering, SCM-Arena places models in the role of ordering agents across a four-tier supply chain simulation derived from the Beer Game with varying demand patterns, information visibility, decision memory, and prompt framing conditions. Performance is assessed through cost ratio relative to a human baseline, demand amplification (bullwhip effect), and behavioral descriptors of ordering coordination and decision complexity. Aggregated results are publicly accessible at scm-arena.com. This paper describes the protocol design, metrics, and platform.

UpstreamBench: A 7,440-Question LLM Benchmark for Expert Upstream Petroleum and Subsurface Reasoning
authors: Rong Lu
abstract: UpstreamBench v0.1 is an expert-style multiple-choice benchmark for evaluating LLMs on upstream petroleum engineering, geoscience, geophysics, petrophysics, drilling, completions, production, geomechanics, and adjacent subsurface workflows. The benchmark contains exactly 7,440 source-linked questions: 20 mechanically validated accepted items from each of 372 technical reference books. UpstreamBench scales the earlier FormationEval benchmark and complements PetroBench with broader book-level coverage, per-source answer balancing, line-level evidence traceability, and an exact nine-model locally hosted evaluation. Its design follows the Citius, Altius, Fortius principle of a faster reproducible pipeline, higher full-corpus coverage, and stronger validation and failure accounting.

title: Are LLM-Agent Prompt-Injection Benchmarks Still Valid? A Cross-Model and Cross-Benchmark Study
authors: Sushil Khairnar
abstract:
Abstract 
                 Indirect prompt injection is the leading security problem for tool-using LLM agents, and a growing number of benchmarks have been developed to measure the robustness of the agents and the effectiveness of defenses against it. This work highlights an essential question which is often ignored in the research community: Is it true that these benchmarks are still applicable for current models, and is the robustness demonstrated on one benchmark portable to another benchmark, another vendor, or to another defense strategy? Using a unified, faithful, and configurable harness, we evaluate the attack success rate (ASR) of 11 models from five different vendors (Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Mistral, DeepSeek) on two single-shot benchmarks with different threat models - InjecAgent (tool hijacking) and a targeted BIPIA-email injection (benign content insertion) and on the agent benchmark AgentDojo for four vendors, together with the evaluation of defense on ten models. Our findings show three primary results. First, benchmark saturation is vendor-specific: InjecAgent achieves 0% ASR on the Claude family of models, while other vendors are still vulnerable to attacks at rates ranging from 16% to 76%, indicating that the benchmark is only solved for Anthropic models. Second, the two single-shot benchmarks give conflicting evaluations of the robustness of the same models (e.g., Claude Opus 5 scores 0% ASR on InjecAgent, yet 59% on BIPIA). They have negatively correlated robustness ranking (Kendall’s τ = −0.24, permutation p = 0.41, underpowered with 11 models) and five out of eleven models are rated secure on one benchmark but vulnerable on the other. Third, none of the examined prompt-based defenses works universally across models.

title: Do Hindi LLM Benchmarks Agree? A Cross-benchmark Consistency Study and the Case for Harmonized Evaluation
authors: Prince Kumar
abstract: The rapid proliferation of evaluation benchmarks for Hindi and other Indic languages raises a fundamental question: do different benchmarks agree on the relative quality of the same language models? We investigate this question across seven Hindi LLM benchmarks covering natural language inference, sentiment classification, exam-style knowledge, mathematical reasoning, factual question answering, instruction-following, and functioncalling. We find strong and statistically significant cross-benchmark agreement (Kendall's W = 0.79, p = 0.0002) across five evaluated language models, while the benchmark with substantially lower pairwise agreement exhibits near-ceiling scores and limited score variation, suggesting a role for benchmark discriminability in cross-benchmark rank comparisons. A smaller Bengali validation subset also shows significant concordance (Kendall's W = 0.864, p = 0.035), providing additional evidence that the observed agreement pattern extends beyond the Hindi evaluation while remaining limited in benchmark coverage. We further introduce a 120-item regional Hindi diagnostic covering Standard Hindi, Awadhi, Bhojpuri, and Braj across the same five-model panel. The Standard Hindi subset produces the same model ordering as mean performance across the three nonstandard varieties (ρ = 1.00), yet item-level analysis reveals 22 standard-correct-to-varietywrong transitions among 450 paired comparisons, compared with 7 transitions in the reverse direction. These results distinguish ranklevel consistency from item-level invariance. Finally, we identify six concrete measurement artifacts encountered during benchmark construction and analysis. We correct five, involving script-encoding errors, token-budget truncation, JSON-schema mismatches, vocabularycoverage gaps in automated scoring, and checkpointing issues, while leaving one unresolved mismatch between English-designed exacttoken-match evaluation and Hindi's productive compound-word morphology as a documented linguistic limitation. Together, these findings motivate a discriminability-aware, harmonized reporting protocol for future Hindi and Indic LLM evaluation.

title: Executing the Output: An Execution-Scored Benchmark of LLM-Generated Neutron Shielding Inputs Across Three Vendors
authors: Alan Halley
abstract:
We benchmark large language models on a task whose ground truth cannot be argued with: write a complete OpenMC input script for a neutron shielding problem, run it, and compare the answer with a published reference. Five natural-language specifications, ordered by physical complexity, were given single-shot, with no tools and no error feedback, to eight frontier models from three vendors and one open-weight model: 135 samples, and every complete script was executed (four samples were refusals; three were cut off by our own token cap and not run). 

Four observations stand out. At three samples per model per rung they are signals, not rates. First, whether code runs and whether it is right order models differently. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 tie for the most scripts that run on the three non-trivial rungs (7 of 9 each), but Opus 5.5 converts four of them into physically correct answers and Astra two. Second, the failures that stopped scripts were API details, and some of them are durable. One pair of individually valid library calls, a thermal-scattering table attached to water and then water passed to a mixing routine, defeated 6 of 6 samples in the August matrix and 8 of 21 in the September one, in models from all three vendors and both Claude generations. Third, a newer model is not monotonically more usable. Claude Opus 5.5 refused all three samples of the conversationally worded rung, flagged by the provider’s filter as “cyber” content, where Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.5 answered the same prompt. Fourth, most of these failures surfaced only because the scripts were run, and the same was true of our own instrument: we log 29 defects in it, and the most consequential were found only because a number came out wrong. 

A one-turn repair arm, in which each failed script is shown its own error once, passes 11 of 21 frontier-model failures and clears the mixing defect in 7 of 7 decidable cases. An open-weight model passed nothing, single-shot or repaired.

title: Towards Effective Offensive Security LLM Agents: Hyperparameter Tuning, LLM as a Judge, and a Lightweight CTF Benchmark
authors: Minghao Shao; Nanda Rani; Kimberly Milner; Haoran Xi; Meet Udeshi; Saksham Aggarwal; Venkata Sai Charan Putrevu; Sandeep K. Shukla; Prashanth Krishnamurthy; Farshad Khorrami; Ramesh Karri; Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Recent advances in LLM agentic systems have improved the automation of offensive security tasks, particularly for Capture the Flag (CTF) challenges. We systematically investigate the key factors that drive agent success and provide a detailed recipe for building effective LLM-based offensive security agents. First, we present CTFJudge, a framework leveraging LLM as a judge to analyze agent trajectories and provide granular evaluation across CTF solving steps. Second, we propose a novel metric, CTF Competency Index (CCI) for partial correctness, revealing how closely agent solutions align with human-crafted gold standards. Third, we examine how LLM hyperparameters, namely temperature, top-p, and maximum token length, influence agent performance and automated cybersecurity task planning. For rapid evaluation, we present CTFTiny, a curated benchmark of 50 representative CTF challenges across binary exploitation, web, reverse engineering, forensics, and cryptography. Our findings identify optimal multi-agent coordination settings and lay the groundwork for future LLM agent research in cybersecurity.

title: Semantic Method Naming and LLM Agent Accuracy: A Controlled Benchmark of REST/CRUD versus Agentic API Design
authors: Chris Hood
abstract:
As large language models take on AI agent roles, the design of the APIs they invoke becomes a measurable variable in task success. We investigate whether semantically rich method names aligned with user intent (BOOK, FIND, QUERY) produce higher endpoint selection accuracy than conventional REST/CRUD verbs (POST /reservations, GET /restaurants/search).

We developed the Agentic API Test Lab, a controlled benchmark with 36 natural-language tasks evaluated against a catalog of 24 CRUD and 21 agentic endpoint pairs. We conducted 7,200 trials across four LLM families (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok-3, GPT-4o, Llama 3.2 3B) spanning 18 experimental conditions.

In mixed-paradigm conditions, agentic methods outperform CRUD by 10–29 percentage points across all three frontier models (aggregate z = 3.77, p < 0.001). The effect is entirely absent in Llama 3.2 (0 pp, p = 0.95), establishing a capability threshold near 3B parameters. A description-swap ablation reveals the mechanism: CRUD endpoints given agentic-style descriptions collapse 39–43 pp (p < 0.001), while agentic endpoints given CRUD descriptions decline only 1–15 pp. Confidence calibration error spikes to +60–67 pp under description mismatch, indicating severe overconfidence precisely when models are most wrong.

API method naming is a measurable engineering variable with direct accuracy and safety consequences at frontier scale. The mechanism is not documentation quality but the method name itself, which encodes intent with sufficient density to survive documentation noise.

title: An AI4Research Scoring Benchmark: Characterizing and Calibrating LLM Evaluation of Automated Research Protocols
authors: Yang Yichen; Lin Dianqing; Chaolu Meng
abstract: Automated research (AI4Research) increasingly delegates both generation and evaluation of scientific content to large language models (LLMs). Evaluation of AI-generated experimental protocols still relies on LLM-as-judge scoring, whose systematic inflation threatens the reliability of research automation. To characterize this problem, we construct a benchmark that stress-tests three families of mainstream LLM usage: fifteen agent reasoning frameworks, five reinforcement-learning strategies (PPO, GRPO, GSPO, DAPO, and ODP), and retrieval-augmented generation with dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval. We contribute a methodology-centric dataset of 4,946 peer-reviewed machine-learning papers annotated through a six-stage progressive scheme with Long Chain-of-Thought formatting, and fine-tune 14 representative LLMs as generators. We further test the benchmark on biomedical research problems, a knowledge-intensive non-ML domain, and find that score inflation is amplified precisely where factual grounding is weakest. Across all settings we characterize five manifestations of score inflation, including self-evaluation bias and score-quality decoupling. Grounded in these findings, we propose a staged protocol-generation framework combining persistent memory files, stepwise generation, and dual-judge plus human-expert cross-validation. This framework reduces the mean deviation between LLM-judge and human-expert scores to 10.3 points, less than half the 21 to 26 point deviation of every other approach, yielding protocols that approach expert judgment.

title: OptiMatLLM: A Benchmark Suite and a Lightweight Domain-Specific LLM for Optical Materials Research
authors: Xinyi Wang; Youle Wang; Lei Zhang
abstract: The design of optical materials relies on highly specialized knowledge, which creates a major bottleneck for data-driven scientific discovery in the optical material domain. Large language models open new possibilities for scientific research, but general-purpose models struggle with the domainspecific physical logic and terminology. More importantly, no standardized evaluation benchmark exists to systematically assess how well LLMs perform on optical materials tasks. To fill this gap, we first construct two evaluation benchmarks, Optic_Choice and Optic_QA, designed specifically for the optical materials domain. We build a high-quality instruction-tuning dataset of 23,225 question-answer pairs through an automated multi-stage pipeline from a curated corpus of papers and textbook. We then develop OptiMatLLM, a 7-billion-parameter LLM fine-tuned LLM on this corpus. Evaluation results show that OptiMatLLM achieves top performance on our optical benchmarks, reaching 0.79 accuracy on Optic_Choice, while also performing competitively on broader scientific tests such as CMHChem, ChemBench, and MaScQA. The model retains strong general capabilities as well, scoring 0.91 on the GSM8K mathematical reasoning benchmark. We further provide a systematic comparison of multiple leading models on these benchmarks, establishing a reference for future work. All benchmarks, dataset, and model are publicly released to support further research on LLMs for optical and optoelectronic materials design.

title: Comparative Analysis of Rule-Based, Deep Learning, and LLM Approaches for Causality Extraction: A Unified Benchmark
authors: Albert Schulle
abstract:
Abstract 
                 Causality extraction—the identification of cause–effect relations in natural language text—has been approached through three successive methodological paradigms: rule-based systems relying on lexical and syntactic cues, deep learning models exploiting neural architectures and pre-trained encoders, and, most recently, large language models (LLMs) applied through prompting or fine-tuning. Each paradigm has been evaluated on different datasets, under different annotation schemes, and with different metrics, making it difficult to determine how far apparent performance differences reflect genuine methodological advantages rather than benchmark artifacts. This study addresses that problem by constructing a unified benchmark for comparative evaluation of rule-based, deep learning, and LLM approaches to causality extraction. We consolidate multiple existing corpora—covering news, biomedical, and safety-incident text—into a harmonized annotation format, re-annotate a stratified subset to ensure consistent treatment of implicit and explicit causal relations, and evaluate representative methods from each paradigm under identical preprocessing, train–test splits, and evaluation protocols. We report span-level precision, recall, and F1, document-level F1, calibration error, inference cost, and annotation efficiency, and we conduct cross-domain transfer experiments to assess generalization. Results are analyzed to disentangle the contributions of architecture, training data, and task formulation, with particular attention to the conditions under which each paradigm retains a comparative advantage. We further examine error profiles across paradigms, identifying whether failures are concentrated in explicit versus implicit relations, local versus distributed constructions, and domain-specific versus general-language contexts.

title: Auditing LLM Chemical Priors for Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization of Chemical Reactions: A Validity, Alignment, and Diversity Benchmark
authors: Fan Zhang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed as priors for cold-starting Bayesian optimization (BO) of chemical reactions, yet their benefit–risk profile in multi-objective reaction optimization remains poorly characterized. We present a systematic benchmark asking when LLM knowledge helps, is neutral, or hurts multi-objective BO (MOBO). Across seven public reaction benchmarks (6,384 candidate experiments), we compare nine strategies—including LLM-initialized BO, an LLM-only initializer, and established baselines (TSEMO, EDBO+-style scalarization, LLAMBO)—with 20 seeds per configuration (1,120 main-grid plus 360 ablation campaigns), scored by hypervolume completion and its sampling-efficiency integral (AUC), with paired Wilcoxon tests and two-family Benjamini–Hochberg correction against a random-init BO control. Three regimes emerge. On Suzuki–Miyaura, LLM initialization significantly improves sampling efficiency (ΔAUC +2.0 points, q = 0.026; alternative backbone +2.7 points, q = 1.4 × 10⁻⁴). On Buchwald–Hartwig, LLM priors are statistically indistinguishable from random. On a process-development coupling, LLM initialization significantly harms efficiency (ΔAUC −11.1 points, q = 0.0016) despite a 0% out-of-pool rate, whereas the Suzuki benefit coexists with a 45% out-of-pool rate—the prior’s direction, not its syntactic validity, controls the outcome. Diversity-based initialization (farthest point sampling) matches or exceeds LLM initialization wherever LLMs help, and no LLM-derived benefit exceeds what the knowledge-free diversity control already provides. A five-category diagnostic protocol intercepts 100% out-of-pool suggestions on the flow cases at zero experimental cost. LLM priors are not yet a reliable default for multi-objective reaction optimization; we provide a cost-free pre-campaign screening heuristic for deciding when to trust them.
